query_text: Write the history of a colour.

messages.content: Write the history of a colour.

message.content:
**Colour** has no single history, because its story is really the history of how humans have **seen, named, mixed, and used pigments** over time. From prehistoric cave art to modern digital screens, colour has moved from a scarce natural resource to a highly engineered part of daily life.[1][3][6]

The earliest known use of colour in art goes back more than **40,000 years**, when people mixed materials like **soil, chalk, burnt charcoal, and animal fat** to make simple pigments.[1][3] These early palettes were limited, but they were powerful: black, white, red, yellow, and brown formed the basic colour set for much of early human art.[1][3] Among these, **red ochre** was especially important and appears to have been one of the first pigments used by humans.[1][2][4]

In ancient civilizations, colour became more than decoration. It was tied to **symbolism, status, religion, and technology**.[2][6] Egyptians developed some of the earliest **synthetic pigments**, including **Egyptian blue**, made by heating minerals such as lime, silica, natron, and copper.[2] Other prized colours, such as **lapis lazuli blue** and **Tyrian purple**, were rare and expensive, making them markers of wealth and power.[2][4] Ancient and medieval cultures also relied on pigments like **vermilion**, **carmine**, and various earth pigments, even when some of them were toxic or difficult to produce.[2][4][5]

For centuries, colour theory was shaped by philosophy as much as science. In ancient Greece, colour was often understood through ideas about **light, darkness, and the elements**.[7] That changed dramatically in **1704**, when **Isaac Newton** showed that white light is made up of a spectrum of colours and helped establish modern colour theory.[1][4][7] His work turned colour into something measurable and systematic rather than purely symbolic or artistic.[7]

During the **18th and 19th centuries**, colour history accelerated as chemistry transformed pigment production.[2][4][6] Scientists and manufacturers created new synthetic colours that were brighter, cheaper, and more stable than many natural dyes.[2][4] This led to major shifts in art: movements from the **Renaissance** through **Impressionism** were shaped by newly available pigments and expanded palettes.[1][3] In the 19th and 20th centuries, organic pigments and industrial colour production created an unprecedented range of shades.[6]

Colour theory also developed into the systems used today. After Newton, thinkers such as **Goethe** and later **Munsell** refined how colour was organized and described, helping define concepts like **hue, value, and chroma**.[7] These ideas are still important in art, design, printing, and digital media.[7]

In modern life, colour is no longer only a pigment on stone, cloth, or canvas. It is also a **scientific, industrial, and digital system**, controlled through chemistry, standards, and screens.[6][8] What began as red ochre on cave walls has become a global language of perception, design, and technology.[1][6]

- a **timeline**
- a **history of one specific colour** such as red, blue, or purple
